dossier.public_summary: The dip alternates between two depths, shows an extra eclipse and a strong out-of-eclipse wobble, and changes dramatically from sector to sector, with some sectors showing no dip and others an impossibly deep one. This pattern, seen on the target star itself, is best explained by a stellar binary or systematic/false signal folded at half period, not by a 3.5 Earth-radius planet.

reasons.why: Odd and even transits differ with high statistical significance and a real ~12% depth difference, the classic signature of an eclipsing binary being folded at half its true period rather than a planet at 2.62 d. The signal also has a significant secondary at phase 0.4262 (snr=13.11, depth_ppm=106.2, depth_over_dip=0.04307) and a large phase-curve swing (amplitude_ppm=334.1, chi2=545.7 dof=9).
Depth is not constant across sectors as required for a planet; it varies by factors larger than any aperture effect.

The depth changes significantly even within the same light-curve product, with measurements from 170 ppm to 3363 ppm including negative values (-1902 to -621 ppm), indicating the dip is not a steady astrophysical transit.

Duration is longer than central and fitted with a high impact parameter (b=0.9495) and stellar-density penalty star_density_penalty=55620, matching a grazing/variability-eclipse shape rather than a planet transit, even though shape.v_sigma=-19.34 appears flat-bottomed.
reasons.value: tic_radius=0.63 vs Gaia FLAME=0.748 rad, duration.ratio=1.611 (obs=2.998 h vs central=1.861 h), duration ratio 1.36 with Gaia radius, fit_b=0.9495
